title: Signal Transduction & Second Messengers
summary: The intracellular cascades that turn receptor activation into a cellular response.

lessons.title: G Proteins and Effector Enzymes

levels.kid:
Imagine a doorbell on the outside of a house. When a visitor (a hormone or a medicine) presses it, a little messenger inside the house runs off to tell everyone.

That inside messenger is called a **G protein**. It's like a switch. When the doorbell is pressed, the switch turns **on** and runs to a machine inside the cell to start a job. After a short while, the switch turns itself **off** again.

There are different kinds of G proteins. Some tell the cell to **speed up**, some tell it to **slow down**, and some tell it to **squeeze**. That's how one doorbell can make a heart beat faster or a muscle tighten.
levels.hs:
Many drugs and hormones act on **G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs)**, the largest family of drug targets. A GPCR snakes through the cell membrane seven times. Outside, it binds a messenger such as adrenaline. Inside, it activates a **G protein**.

A G protein has three parts: **alpha, beta and gamma**. When resting, the alpha part holds a molecule called **GDP**. When the receptor is activated, alpha swaps GDP for **GTP**, switches on, and separates from beta-gamma. Both pieces can then turn on effector proteins. Alpha slowly breaks GTP back down to GDP, which turns it off. This built-in timer keeps signals short.

The three main types:
- **Gs (stimulatory)**: turns on **adenylyl cyclase**, raising cAMP. Example: beta receptors in the heart.
- **Gi (inhibitory)**: turns adenylyl cyclase **off**, lowering cAMP. Example: alpha-2 receptors and opioid receptors.
- **Gq**: turns on **phospholipase C**, raising calcium inside the cell. Example: alpha-1 receptors that tighten blood vessels.

Some bacterial toxins hijack G proteins. **Cholera toxin** locks Gs in the "on" position, so gut cells pump out salt and water, causing severe diarrhea.

Knowing a receptor's G protein lets you predict what a drug acting on it will do.
levels.college:
**GPCRs** are seven-transmembrane receptors that act as **guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs)** for heterotrimeric G proteins. Agonist binding stabilizes an active conformation that opens the Gα nucleotide pocket, releasing GDP; GTP (abundant in cells) binds, and Gα-GTP dissociates from Gβγ. Signaling ends when Gα's intrinsic GTPase hydrolyzes GTP, a step accelerated by **RGS proteins** (GTPase-activating proteins).

Major Gα families and effectors:
- **Gαs**: activates adenylyl cyclase → cAMP↑. Receptors: β1, β2, β3, D1, H2, V2, glucagon, TSH, PTH, prostacyclin (IP).
- **Gαi/o**: inhibits adenylyl cyclase; Gβγ opens **GIRK** (Kir3) K+ channels and inhibits N- and P/Q-type Ca2+ channels. Receptors: α2, M2, D2, μ/δ/κ opioid, GABA-B, 5-HT1, adenosine A1, CB1.
- **Gαq/11**: activates phospholipase Cβ → IP3 and DAG. Receptors: α1, M1, M3, H1, V1, AT1, 5-HT2, ETA, oxytocin.
- **Gα12/13**: activates RhoGEFs → RhoA/ROCK (smooth muscle contraction, cytoskeleton).

A classic mnemonic for autonomic and related receptors: "qiss and qiq till you're siq of sqs": α1 q, α2 i, β1 s, β2 s; M1 q, M2 i, M3 q; D1 s, D2 i; H1 q, H2 s; V1 q, V2 s.

**Bacterial toxins** as tools and diseases:
- **Cholera toxin** ADP-ribosylates Gαs (an arginine), blocking GTPase activity: Gs stays on, cAMP rises, CFTR opens, causing secretory diarrhea.
- **Pertussis toxin** ADP-ribosylates Gαi (a cysteine), uncoupling it from receptors: Gi can no longer inhibit adenylyl cyclase, so cAMP also rises.

**Desensitization**: G protein receptor kinases (GRKs) phosphorylate active receptors, **β-arrestins** bind, uncouple the G protein and drive internalization. This underlies tachyphylaxis to β2 agonists.
levels.phd:
Structural biology transformed GPCR pharmacology. The β2-adrenoceptor–Gs crystal structure (Kobilka, 2011; Nobel Prize 2012 with Lefkowitz) showed that activation involves an outward swing of transmembrane helix 6, opening a cytoplasmic cavity into which the Gα C-terminal α5 helix inserts. Cryo-EM has since resolved hundreds of GPCR–G protein complexes, revealing how coupling specificity is encoded by receptor intracellular loops and the Gα C-terminus.

Receptors are not simple on/off switches. They sample multiple conformations, and ligands stabilize different subsets. **Biased agonism** describes ligands that preferentially activate G protein or β-arrestin pathways. This inspired G protein–biased μ-opioid agonists (oliceridine), hoping to retain analgesia with less respiratory depression; clinical separation has been modest, and the original β-arrestin hypothesis for respiratory depression has been challenged. Bias is also system-dependent, influenced by receptor reserve and effector stoichiometry, so it must be quantified carefully (operational model transduction coefficients).

**Allosteric modulators** bind topographically distinct sites. Positive allosteric modulators such as cinacalcet (calcium-sensing receptor) enhance endogenous agonist signaling with a ceiling effect and potential subtype selectivity, because allosteric sites are less conserved than orthosteric ones.

**Gβγ** is a signaling unit in its own right: it gates GIRK channels (vagal slowing of the SA node via M2), inhibits presynaptic Ca2+ channels (opioid and α2 presynaptic inhibition), and activates PLCβ2/3 and PI3Kγ.

Disease genetics confirm pathway logic. Activating GNAS mutations (R201) cause McCune–Albright syndrome when mosaic and drive some pituitary somatotroph adenomas (gsp oncogene). Inactivating GNAS mutations cause pseudohypoparathyroidism with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy. Somatic GNAQ R183Q causes Sturge–Weber syndrome, and GNAQ/GNA11 Q209 mutations drive uveal melanoma.
levels.expert:
Thinking in G protein terms lets you predict effects, adverse effects and antidotes rather than memorize them.

- **β-blocker overdose**: Gs signaling in the heart is blocked. Glucagon acts on its own Gs-coupled receptor and raises cAMP, bypassing the blockade. High-dose insulin euglycemic therapy, catecholamines and PDE3 inhibitors are other ways to restore inotropy.
- **Receptor selectivity determines adverse effects.** Phenylephrine (α1, Gq) raises blood pressure with reflex bradycardia. Dobutamine (mainly β1, Gs) increases contractility. Clonidine (α2, Gi) reduces central sympathetic outflow; abrupt withdrawal causes rebound hypertension because downstream adaptations persist.
- **Opioids**: μ receptors couple to Gi/o. Gβγ opens GIRK channels and inhibits presynaptic calcium channels, reducing neurotransmitter release. That same mechanism in the brainstem respiratory network causes respiratory depression. Tolerance involves receptor phosphorylation, β-arrestin recruitment and cAMP superactivation; abrupt withdrawal produces a hyperadrenergic state.
- **Tachyphylaxis**: repeated β2 agonist use in asthma causes receptor desensitization, part of why inhaled corticosteroids, which up-regulate β2 receptor expression, are combined with them.
- **Vasopressin**: V1 (Gq) on vascular smooth muscle causes vasoconstriction, used in septic shock; V2 (Gs) in collecting ducts inserts aquaporin-2. Desmopressin is V2-selective (diabetes insipidus, bleeding disorders); vaptans block V2 to treat hyponatremia (SIADH).
- **Neurosurgery relevance**: GH-secreting pituitary adenomas often carry gsp mutations; somatostatin analogs (octreotide, lanreotide; Gi-coupled SST2/SST5) reduce GH secretion when surgery is incomplete. Dopamine agonists (D2, Gi) shrink prolactinomas, often without surgery.

RGS proteins, GRKs and arrestins are emerging targets, but nearly a third of approved drugs already act on GPCRs.

keyPoints: GPCRs (7TM) act as GEFs: Gα swaps GDP for GTP and separates from Gβγ
Gα's GTPase ends the signal; RGS proteins accelerate it
Gs → adenylyl cyclase ↑cAMP; Gi → ↓cAMP, Gβγ opens GIRK; Gq → PLCβ → IP3/DAG; G12/13 → Rho
Cholera toxin locks Gs on; pertussis toxin uncouples Gi; both raise cAMP
GRKs and β-arrestins desensitize receptors (tachyphylaxis); biased agonism exploits pathway differences

test.q: How many times does a typical GPCR cross the cell membrane?
test.explain: GPCRs are seven-transmembrane (7TM) receptors.

test.q: What turns a G protein alpha subunit ON?
test.explain: Receptor activation catalyzes GDP release; GTP binding activates Gα.

test.q: What turns a G protein alpha subunit OFF?
choices: Its intrinsic GTPase hydrolyzes GTP to GDP
test.explain: GTP hydrolysis (accelerated by RGS proteins) returns Gα to the inactive GDP state.

test.q: Gs-coupled receptors activate which enzyme?
test.explain: Gαs stimulates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP.

test.q: α1-adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle couple to:
test.explain: α1 → Gq → phospholipase C → IP3 and DAG → Ca2+ → contraction.

test.q: μ-opioid receptors couple to which G protein family?
test.explain: Opioid receptors are Gi/o-coupled: lower cAMP, open GIRK channels, inhibit presynaptic calcium channels.

test.q: Cholera toxin causes massive watery diarrhea by:
choices: Locking Gαs in the active state, raising cAMP
Blocking Gαq and lowering IP3 and calcium
Inhibiting adenylyl cyclase in gut cells
Activating Gαi, which opens chloride pores
test.explain: ADP-ribosylation of Gαs blocks its GTPase, so cAMP stays high and CFTR secretes chloride.

test.q: Which receptor is Gs-coupled?
test.explain: β1 → Gs. M2 and α2 are Gi; H1 is Gq.

test.q: Name the proteins that bind phosphorylated GPCRs, uncouple G proteins and drive internalization.
test.explain: After GRK phosphorylation, β-arrestins cause desensitization and internalization.

test.q: RGS proteins speed up GTP hydrolysis, so they act as GTPase-___ proteins.
test.explain: RGS proteins are GAPs that shorten G protein signaling.

test.q: Gβγ released from Gi opens ___ potassium channels, slowing the heart.
test.explain: G protein–gated inwardly rectifying K+ channels hyperpolarize SA node cells after M2 activation.

kidTest.q: In the doorbell story, what is the G protein?
kidTest.explain: The G protein carries the message inside the cell.

kidTest.q: What happens to the G protein switch after a while?
kidTest.explain: G proteins have a built-in timer to switch off.

kidTest.q: Can different G proteins tell cells to do different jobs?
choices: Yes, like speed up, slow down or squeeze
No, all of them do the very same job
kidTest.explain: Gs, Gi and Gq send different messages.

kidTest.q: Who presses the doorbell?
kidTest.explain: Messengers outside the cell bind the receptor.

kidTest.q: The G protein is like a light ___ that turns on and off.
kidTest.explain: G proteins switch on (GTP) and off (GDP).

advancedTest.q: Pertussis toxin raises cAMP by a different route than cholera toxin. It:
choices: ADP-ribosylates Gαi so it cannot couple to receptors
Locks Gαs in the GTP state
advancedTest.explain: Uncoupled Gi can no longer inhibit adenylyl cyclase, so cAMP rises.

advancedTest.q: Glucagon is used in β-blocker overdose because it:
choices: Activates its own Gs-coupled receptor, raising cardiac cAMP independently of β receptors
Competitively displaces the β-blocker from cardiac β1 receptors at high levels
Blocks phosphodiesterase 3, which stops cAMP breakdown in heart muscle
Inhibits Gi proteins, which removes the brake on adenylyl cyclase
advancedTest.explain: Bypassing the blocked β receptor restores cAMP-dependent inotropy and chronotropy.

advancedTest.q: A G protein–biased μ-opioid agonist was designed to:
choices: Favor β-arrestin over G-protein signaling to limit opioid tolerance
Preferentially activate G protein over β-arrestin signaling, hoping to reduce adverse effects
Block the μ receptor while still giving analgesia via κ receptors
Signal mainly through Gq coupling, raising IP3 and calcium in pain neurons
advancedTest.explain: Oliceridine exemplifies biased agonism; clinical separation from respiratory depression has been modest.

advancedTest.q: Activating somatic GNAS (Gαs) mutations in mosaic form cause:
advancedTest.explain: Constitutive Gs signaling causes café-au-lait spots, fibrous dysplasia and endocrine hyperfunction. Inactivating GNAS causes pseudohypoparathyroidism; GNAQ mutations cause Sturge–Weber and uveal melanoma.

lessons.title: cAMP and Protein Kinase A

levels.kid:
When adrenaline rings the doorbell on a heart cell, the switch inside turns on a little machine. That machine makes lots of tiny messenger molecules called **cAMP**.

cAMP is like a whistle that wakes up a team of workers called **PKA**. The PKA workers run around the cell sticking little flags on other proteins, which tells them to work harder. In the heart, that means beating **stronger and faster**.

One doorbell press makes many cAMP whistles, and each wakes many workers. So a tiny signal becomes a big response!

Another helper, **PDE**, eats up the cAMP whistles so the cell can calm down.
levels.hs:
**Cyclic AMP (cAMP)** is one of the most important **second messengers**: molecules that carry a signal from a receptor at the cell surface to targets inside the cell.

Here's the pathway:
1. A hormone binds a Gs-coupled receptor (like adrenaline on a beta receptor).
2. Gs activates **adenylyl cyclase**, an enzyme that turns ATP into cAMP.
3. cAMP activates **protein kinase A (PKA)**.
4. PKA adds phosphate groups to other proteins (**phosphorylation**), switching them on or off.

What PKA does depends on the cell:
- **Heart**: stronger and faster contractions.
- **Airway smooth muscle**: relaxation, opening the airways (how albuterol works in asthma).
- **Liver**: breaking down glycogen into glucose.
- **Kidney**: inserting water channels so the body saves water (vasopressin).

The signal is switched off by enzymes called **phosphodiesterases (PDEs)**, which break cAMP down. Drugs that block PDEs keep cAMP high. Caffeine and theophylline weakly block PDEs, and milrinone blocks PDE3 to strengthen the heart.

The pathway also **amplifies**: one receptor activates many G proteins, each adenylyl cyclase makes many cAMP molecules, and each PKA phosphorylates many proteins. A few hormone molecules can change a whole cell's behavior.
levels.college:
**Adenylyl cyclases** (nine membrane isoforms, AC1–9, plus soluble AC10) convert ATP to cAMP and pyrophosphate. Gαs stimulates all membrane isoforms; Gαi inhibits several; isoform-specific regulation by Ca2+/calmodulin, Gβγ and PKC adds integration. **Forskolin** directly activates AC1–8, a research tool.

**PKA** is a tetramer of two regulatory (R) and two catalytic (C) subunits. Each R subunit binds two cAMP molecules, releasing active C subunits that phosphorylate serine and threonine residues in R-R-X-S/T motifs. **A-kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs)** tether PKA near its substrates, creating local signaling compartments.

Other cAMP effectors:
- **EPAC** (exchange protein directly activated by cAMP) activates the small GTPase Rap1.
- **HCN channels** (hyperpolarization-activated, cyclic nucleotide-gated) carry the pacemaker current If in the SA node. cAMP binding shifts their activation, so β1 stimulation increases heart rate. **Ivabradine** blocks If.

Cardiac PKA targets:
- L-type Ca2+ channels: more Ca2+ entry → inotropy.
- **Phospholamban**: phosphorylation relieves its inhibition of SERCA2a → faster Ca2+ reuptake (lusitropy) and larger SR stores.
- Troponin I: reduced myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity → faster relaxation.
- Ryanodine receptor 2: altered Ca2+ release.

In smooth muscle, cAMP/PKA phosphorylates and inhibits myosin light chain kinase and lowers intracellular Ca2+, causing relaxation (β2 bronchodilation, prostacyclin vasodilation). In platelets, cAMP inhibits aggregation.

**Transcription**: PKA phosphorylates **CREB** at Ser133, recruiting CBP/p300 to cAMP response elements. This underlies long-term changes such as memory consolidation.

**PDEs** (11 families) terminate signaling: PDE3 (heart, platelets, vascular smooth muscle: milrinone, cilostazol), PDE4 (inflammatory cells: roflumilast, apremilast), PDE5 (cGMP-specific: sildenafil), and nonselective methylxanthines.
levels.phd:
cAMP signaling is not a uniformly diffusing cytosolic signal. FRET-based biosensors revealed that cAMP is **compartmentalized** into nanodomains, shaped by localized PDEs acting as sinks, AKAP-assembled signalosomes, and the relatively restricted effective diffusion of cAMP in cells. This explains a long-standing paradox: in cardiomyocytes, β1-adrenergic and PGE2 receptors both raise global cAMP, yet only β1 stimulation produces robust inotropy, because each receptor generates cAMP in different microdomains with different PKA substrates nearby.

β1 and β2 receptors differ in compartmentation. β1 signaling is broadly distributed and strongly couples to phospholamban and L-type channel phosphorylation. β2 signaling is localized to T-tubules and caveolae, and β2 can also couple to Gi, limiting its inotropic effect and activating protective pathways. In failing hearts this organization breaks down, as β2 receptors redistribute and chronic β1–cAMP signaling becomes maladaptive: CaMKII activation, apoptosis and arrhythmia. That provides a mechanistic rationale for the mortality benefit of β-blockers in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and the excess mortality seen with chronic oral PDE3 inhibitors and other inotropes.

Receptors also signal from **endosomes**. After internalization, some GPCRs (β2AR, TSH receptor, PTH receptor) sustain cAMP production from endosomal compartments, producing distinct transcriptional outcomes. For the PTH receptor, differences in sustained (endosomal) versus transient signaling are proposed to explain why PTH and abaloparatide act differently on bone.

PDE isoform diversity (over 100 splice variants) creates targetable specificity. PDE4 subtypes (A–D) and their scaffolding interactions differ between tissues; PDE4D inhibition causes emesis, limiting nonselective PDE4 inhibitors, while allosteric PDE4B-preferring and PDE4D-sparing compounds are in development. PDE4B is a target in pulmonary fibrosis, and nerandomilast was reported to slow of lung function decline in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis trials.
levels.expert:
The cAMP pathway runs straight through acute care.

- **Shock and heart failure.** β1 agonists (dobutamine) and PDE3 inhibitors (milrinone) both raise cardiac cAMP. Milrinone works even when β receptors are blocked or down-regulated, and it also dilates vessels (an "inodilator"), so hypotension and arrhythmias limit it. It is renally cleared and accumulates in kidney failure. Chronic oral PDE3 inhibition increased mortality in heart failure, which is why these drugs are short-term or bridge therapies. Cilostazol, another PDE3 inhibitor used for claudication, is contraindicated in heart failure for the same reason.
- **β-blocker or calcium channel blocker overdose.** Glucagon (Gs via its own receptor) and PDE3 inhibitors raise cAMP independently of β receptors; high-dose insulin improves myocardial energy use.
- **Asthma and COPD.** β2 agonists (Gs → cAMP → PKA) relax airway smooth muscle; theophylline's narrow therapeutic index (seizures, arrhythmias) limits it, and roflumilast (PDE4) reduces exacerbations in severe COPD with chronic bronchitis, but causes weight loss, nausea and psychiatric effects.
- **Platelets.** Prostacyclin (IP receptor → Gs) and dipyridamole (PDE and adenosine reuptake inhibition) raise platelet cAMP and reduce aggregation.
- **Water balance.** V2 → Gs → PKA → aquaporin-2 insertion. Lithium impairs this and causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Tolvaptan blocks V2 to treat hyponatremia, but sodium must rise slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.
- **Neuro.** Adenosine A2A receptors (Gs) in the striatum are targeted by istradefylline in Parkinson's disease. Caffeine's CNS effects are mainly adenosine receptor antagonism, not PDE inhibition, at normal exposures. Theophylline toxicity causes refractory seizures, a neurocritical care concern.

For exam-style questions, remember: anything that raises cAMP in heart muscle increases contractility; anything that raises cAMP in smooth muscle or platelets relaxes or inhibits them.

keyPoints: Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA (R2C2; cAMP frees catalytic subunits)
Other cAMP targets: EPAC, HCN channels (If); CREB drives transcription
Heart: PKA phosphorylates L-type channels, phospholamban and troponin I (inotropy, lusitropy)
Smooth muscle and platelets: cAMP relaxes and inhibits (β2 agonists, prostacyclin)
PDEs end signaling: PDE3 (milrinone, cilostazol), PDE4 (roflumilast), methylxanthines nonselective

kidTest.explain: The machine makes lots of cAMP messengers.

Gobble up the whole cell for a snack
Stick little flags on proteins to make them work

kidTest.explain: cAMP and PKA boost heart contractions.

Eats up cAMP so the cell calms down

advancedTest.q: In cardiomyocytes, both β1 and PGE2 receptors raise global cAMP, but only β1 strongly increases contractility. Best explanation:
choices: cAMP is compartmentalized into nanodomains with different nearby PKA targets
PGE2 receptors are Gq-coupled and lower cAMP near the myofilaments
PGE2 directly destroys PKA so its cAMP signal can't be read by the cell
β1 receptors act through Gi and PI3 kinase rather than cAMP–PKA signaling

advancedTest.q: Chronic oral PDE3 inhibition in heart failure:
choices: Cured heart failure, so it became first-line long-term therapy
Increased mortality, so PDE3 inhibitors are used short-term only
Reduced mortality to a similar degree as β-blockers do
Left mortality unchanged while reducing hospitalizations modestly

advancedTest.q: Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus mainly by impairing:
choices: Proximal tubule sodium reabsorption via the Na+/H+ exchanger
Renin release from the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney
V2 receptor–cAMP–aquaporin-2 signaling in the collecting duct
Glomerular filtration, by constricting the afferent arteriole
advancedTest.explain: Lithium enters principal cells via ENaC and disrupts cAMP-dependent aquaporin-2 expression and trafficking.

advancedTest.q: β2-adrenoceptors in cardiomyocytes limit their own inotropic effect partly because they can also couple to:
advancedTest.explain: Dual Gs/Gi coupling restricts β2 cAMP signaling and activates protective pathways.

lessons.title: Phospholipase C, IP3, DAG and Calcium

levels.kid:
Some doorbells on cells use a different switch, called **Gq**. When it turns on, it cuts a fat molecule in the cell's wall into **two messengers**.

The first messenger, **IP3**, floats to a storage room inside the cell full of **calcium**. It unlocks the door, and calcium rushes out.

Calcium is like a starting whistle. It tells muscles to **squeeze** and tells other parts to get to work.

The second messenger, **DAG**, stays in the wall and wakes up a team called **PKC**.

When the job is done, pumps push the calcium back into storage so the cell can relax.
levels.hs:
Gq-coupled receptors use a different second messenger system from cAMP.

1. A hormone or drug binds a **Gq-coupled receptor** (for example, alpha-1 receptors on blood vessels or M3 receptors in the airways).
2. Gq activates the enzyme **phospholipase C (PLC)**.
3. PLC cuts a membrane lipid called **PIP2** into two messengers: **IP3** and **DAG**.
4. **IP3** diffuses to the endoplasmic reticulum and opens IP3 receptor channels, releasing stored **calcium (Ca2+)** into the cytoplasm.
5. **DAG** stays in the membrane and, together with calcium, activates **protein kinase C (PKC)**.

Calcium is a powerful signal. It binds a protein called **calmodulin**, which then activates other enzymes. In smooth muscle, calcium–calmodulin activates **myosin light chain kinase**, causing contraction. That is why alpha-1 agonists like phenylephrine squeeze blood vessels and raise blood pressure.

Calcium also controls neurotransmitter release, hormone secretion and gene expression.

The signal ends when pumps return calcium to storage or push it out of the cell, and when IP3 is broken down.

An important drug link: **lithium**, used in bipolar disorder, interferes with recycling of inositol, which the cell needs to remake PIP2. This is one theory for how lithium calms overactive signaling.
levels.college:
**Gαq/11** activates **phospholipase Cβ (PLCβ)**, which hydrolyzes phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (**PIP2**) into inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (**IP3**) and **diacylglycerol (DAG)**. Receptor tyrosine kinases activate **PLCγ** through SH2-domain docking, so growth factors also use this pathway.

**IP3** binds IP3 receptors (tetrameric Ca2+ channels) on the ER, releasing Ca2+. Depletion of ER stores is sensed by **STIM1**, which activates **Orai1** plasma membrane channels: **store-operated Ca2+ entry (SOCE)**, critical in lymphocytes.

**DAG** recruits and activates PKC. PKC isoforms: conventional (α, βI, βII, γ; need Ca2+ and DAG), novel (δ, ε, η, θ; DAG only) and atypical (ζ, ι/λ; neither). **Phorbol esters** mimic DAG and are potent tumor promoters.

**Ca2+ effectors:**
- **Calmodulin** → CaMKII, myosin light chain kinase (smooth muscle contraction), eNOS, some adenylyl cyclases and PDE1.
- **Calcineurin** (Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase) dephosphorylates **NFAT**, which enters the nucleus and drives IL-2 transcription. Cyclosporine (with cyclophilin) and tacrolimus (with FKBP12) inhibit calcineurin.
- Troponin C (striated muscle), synaptotagmin (vesicle release).

**Termination:** SERCA (ER uptake), PMCA and Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (efflux); IP3 is dephosphorylated by inositol phosphatases. **Lithium** inhibits inositol monophosphatase and inositol polyphosphate 1-phosphatase, depleting free inositol in overactive cells (the inositol depletion hypothesis), and also inhibits GSK-3β.

**Gq receptors with clinical drugs:** α1 (phenylephrine; prazosin and tamsulosin block), M3 (bronchoconstriction, glands; tiotropium blocks), H1 (antihistamines), AT1 (ARBs), V1 (vasopressin in shock), 5-HT2A (atypical antipsychotics block), ETA (bosentan, ambrisentan), oxytocin receptor (labor induction), GnRH and TRH receptors.
levels.phd:
Calcium signals carry information in their **spatial and temporal pattern**, not just their amplitude. IP3 receptors are co-regulated by IP3 and Ca2+ itself, with a bell-shaped Ca2+ dependence: modest Ca2+ elevation sensitizes the receptor (calcium-induced calcium release), while high Ca2+ inhibits it. This positive-then-negative feedback generates elementary events ("blips" and "puffs") that can recruit neighboring clusters into regenerative **Ca2+ waves** and **oscillations**. Downstream decoders read frequency: NFAT translocation integrates oscillation frequency through calcineurin's slow dephosphorylation and kinases' slow rephosphorylation; CaMKII autophosphorylation at Thr286 makes it a frequency detector that can encode memory-like persistence.

PIP2 is not merely a precursor. It directly regulates many ion channels (KCNQ/M-current channels, GIRK, TRP channels). Muscarinic M1 receptor activation depletes PIP2 and closes KCNQ2/3 channels, increasing neuronal excitability; this is a canonical example of lipid signaling in neurons. Retigabine (ezogabine), a KCNQ opener, exploited this channel family for epilepsy before its withdrawal for retinal pigmentation.

The ER Ca2+ store is coupled to mitochondria at contact sites, where IP3R-mediated Ca2+ transfer stimulates mitochondrial dehydrogenases and ATP production, while excess transfer triggers permeability transition and apoptosis. Bcl-2 family proteins regulate IP3 receptors, linking Ca2+ signaling to cell death decisions.

The Ca2+ release mechanism differs in striated muscle. Skeletal muscle uses mechanical coupling between the dihydropyridine receptor (Cav1.1) and ryanodine receptor 1 (RyR1); cardiac muscle uses calcium-induced Ca2+ release via RyR2. Gain-of-function RyR1 variants cause **malignant hyperthermia**, uncontrolled SR Ca2+ release triggered by volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine. **Dantrolene** binds RyR1 and reduces Ca2+ leak. Leaky RyR2 channels contribute to heart failure arrhythmias and catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.
levels.expert:
This pathway explains many drugs used daily in the OR, ICU and clinic.

- **Vasopressors**: phenylephrine (α1) and vasopressin (V1) raise blood pressure through Gq-driven smooth muscle calcium. Vasopressin still works in severe acidosis, when catecholamine receptors respond poorly, which is one reason it is added in septic shock. Norepinephrine combines α1 vasoconstriction with β1 support.
- **Benign prostatic hyperplasia**: α1A blockers (tamsulosin) relax prostate smooth muscle; floppy iris syndrome during cataract surgery is a known complication, because α1A receptors also tone the iris dilator.
- **Bronchospasm and secretions**: M3 antagonists (ipratropium, tiotropium, glycopyrrolate) block Gq-mediated bronchoconstriction and gland secretion.
- **Transplant immunosuppression**: tacrolimus and cyclosporine block calcineurin–NFAT. Their neurotoxicity (tremor, seizures, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome) and nephrotoxicity (afferent vasoconstriction) are frequent issues; levels are monitored, and CYP3A4 and P-gp interactions are common.
- **Lithium**: inositol depletion and GSK-3 inhibition are the leading mechanistic theories. Practically: narrow therapeutic index, renal clearance, interactions with thiazides, ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs, and long-term thyroid, renal and parathyroid effects (hypercalcemia).
- **Malignant hyperthermia**: rising end-tidal CO2, rigidity, tachycardia and hyperthermia under volatile agents or succinylcholine call for stopping triggers and giving dantrolene immediately. Susceptible patients (RyR1 or CACNA1S variants) receive total intravenous anesthesia.
- **Neurosurgery**: subarachnoid hemorrhage vasospasm involves sustained smooth muscle Ca2+ signaling (endothelin, Gq). Nimodipine improves outcomes after aneurysmal SAH, although its benefit is thought to involve neuroprotection more than angiographic vasospasm reversal; clazosentan (an ETA antagonist) reduced vasospasm without consistent functional benefit.

When a drug causes smooth muscle contraction, think Gq and calcium; when it relaxes, think cAMP or cGMP.

keyPoints: Gq → PLCβ → PIP2 cleaved into IP3 (ER Ca2+ release) and DAG (PKC activation)
Ca2+ acts via calmodulin (MLCK, CaMKII, eNOS) and calcineurin (NFAT, IL-2)
Store-operated entry (STIM1/Orai1) refills stores; SERCA, PMCA and NCX end signals
Gq receptors: α1, M1, M3, H1, AT1, V1, 5-HT2A, ETA, oxytocin
Drug links: calcineurin inhibitors, lithium (inositol depletion), dantrolene (RyR1, malignant hyperthermia)

lessons.title: Nitric Oxide and cGMP

levels.kid:
Your blood vessels are like garden hoses with muscles wrapped around them. When the muscles relax, the hose gets wider and blood flows easily.

The cells lining the inside of blood vessels make a tiny gas called **nitric oxide**, or **NO**. NO floats over to the muscle and tells it to **relax**.

Inside the muscle, NO turns on a machine that makes a messenger called **cGMP**. cGMP is the "chill out" signal.

Some heart medicines, like the little pills people put under their tongue for chest pain, work by giving the body extra NO. That opens up the blood vessels so the heart doesn't have to work so hard.
levels.hs:
**Nitric oxide (NO)** is a small gas that acts as a signaling molecule. Its discovery as a messenger in blood vessels won the 1998 Nobel Prize.

How it works in blood vessels:
1. Endothelial cells lining the vessel make NO from the amino acid **arginine**, using the enzyme **nitric oxide synthase (NOS)**. Triggers include blood flow (shear stress), acetylcholine and bradykinin.
2. NO diffuses into the neighboring smooth muscle cells.
3. NO activates **soluble guanylyl cyclase**, which converts GTP into **cyclic GMP (cGMP)**.
4. cGMP activates **protein kinase G (PKG)**, which lowers calcium and makes the muscle relax. The vessel widens (**vasodilation**).

Drugs that use this pathway:
- **Nitroglycerin** and other nitrates release NO. They widen veins especially, which reduces the heart's workload and relieves angina (chest pain).
- **Sildenafil** and **tadalafil** block **PDE5**, the enzyme that breaks down cGMP. They are used for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension.

These two classes must **never be combined**, because together they raise cGMP so much that blood pressure can crash.

The body also makes cGMP another way: heart hormones called **natriuretic peptides** (ANP and BNP) activate a guanylyl cyclase built into their receptor, promoting sodium loss and vasodilation.
levels.college:
**NO synthesis:** NOS converts L-arginine + O2 + NADPH → L-citrulline + NO, requiring tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), FAD, FMN, heme and calmodulin. Three isoforms:
- **nNOS (NOS1)**: neurons; Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent; NO as a neurotransmitter (nitrergic nerves, penile erection, gut relaxation).
- **iNOS (NOS2)**: induced in macrophages by cytokines and LPS; Ca2+-independent, produces large amounts of NO; contributes to septic vasodilation and microbial killing.
- **eNOS (NOS3)**: endothelium; activated by Ca2+/calmodulin and by Akt phosphorylation in response to shear stress.

**Soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC)** is an α/β heterodimer with a reduced (Fe2+) heme. NO binding to the heme activates cGMP synthesis several hundred-fold. **PKG I** then lowers cytosolic Ca2+ (phosphorylating IRAG to inhibit IP3 receptors, activating BKCa channels, enhancing SERCA via phospholamban) and activates myosin light chain phosphatase, causing relaxation. cGMP also gates CNG channels (phototransduction).

**Particulate guanylyl cyclases** are receptors: NPR-A (ANP, BNP), NPR-B (CNP), and GC-C (guanylin, uroguanylin, and E. coli heat-stable enterotoxin). Neprilysin degrades natriuretic peptides; **sacubitril** inhibits neprilysin (combined with valsartan). **Linaclotide** and plecanatide activate GC-C to treat constipation.

**Drugs:**
- **Nitrates**: nitroglycerin requires bioactivation, largely by mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase-2 (ALDH2). Isosorbide mononitrate and dinitrate are longer acting. **Nitroprusside** releases NO spontaneously and also releases cyanide.
- **PDE5 inhibitors**: sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil. Sildenafil's weak PDE6 inhibition causes bluish vision; tadalafil's PDE11 inhibition is linked to back pain and myalgia.
- **sGC stimulators**: riociguat (pulmonary hypertension, CTEPH) and vericiguat (HFrEF) sensitize sGC to NO and stimulate it directly.
- **Inhaled NO**: selective pulmonary vasodilator for persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn.
levels.phd:
NO's biology is governed by its chemistry: a small, uncharged radical that diffuses across membranes with a short biological half-life, limited by reaction with oxyhemoglobin (forming nitrate and methemoglobin) and superoxide. Its reaction with superoxide is diffusion-limited and yields **peroxynitrite**, a strong oxidant and nitrating agent. Endothelial dysfunction in atherosclerosis, diabetes and hypertension reflects reduced NO bioavailability through superoxide scavenging and **eNOS uncoupling**: when BH4 is oxidized or L-arginine scarce, eNOS transfers electrons to O2 and produces superoxide instead of NO, worsening oxidative stress.

sGC exists in redox states. The NO-sensitive form has reduced (Fe2+) heme. Oxidative stress oxidizes the heme to Fe3+ and promotes heme loss, generating NO-insensitive sGC. This motivates two drug classes: **sGC stimulators** (riociguat, vericiguat), which require the reduced heme and act synergistically with NO, and **sGC activators** (cinaciguat, runcaciguat), which target oxidized or heme-free sGC by occupying the heme pocket.

**Nitrate tolerance** has multiple proposed mechanisms: inactivation of ALDH2 by reactive oxygen species formed during bioactivation, neurohormonal counter-regulation (renin–angiotensin and sympathetic activation, plasma volume expansion), and increased vascular superoxide and endothelin. The East Asian **ALDH2*2** variant impairs nitroglycerin bioactivation and is associated with reduced clinical response.

Compartmentation applies to cGMP too: NO-sGC and natriuretic peptide–particulate GC signals regulate different PDEs and effectors in cardiomyocytes. PDE5 preferentially controls the NO-derived pool, while PDE2 and PDE9 regulate natriuretic peptide–derived cGMP. This is one reason PDE5 inhibitors failed to improve heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (RELAX trial), and why PDE9 and sGC-based strategies are explored.

The nitrate–nitrite–NO pathway, via dietary nitrate reduced by oral bacteria, provides an NOS-independent NO source, particularly under hypoxia.
levels.expert:
Clinical NO–cGMP pharmacology centers on vasodilation, its limits and its dangers.

- **Angina and acute coronary syndromes**: sublingual nitroglycerin relieves angina mainly by venodilation (reduced preload and wall stress), with some coronary dilation. Avoid nitrates in right ventricular infarction (preload-dependent), severe aortic stenosis and hypotension, and within the labeled window after a PDE5 inhibitor (longer for tadalafil because of its long half-life). Ask every patient with chest pain about PDE5 inhibitor use before giving nitrates.
- **Tolerance**: continuous nitrate exposure loses effect within a day or so, so long-acting nitrate regimens include a daily nitrate-free interval. Rebound angina can occur during that interval.
- **Acute heart failure and hypertensive emergencies**: IV nitroglycerin reduces pulmonary congestion; nitroprusside is a potent arterial and venous dilator for hypertensive emergencies, but prolonged infusion, especially with renal impairment, risks cyanide and thiocyanate toxicity. Hydroxocobalamin and sodium thiosulfate treat cyanide toxicity.
- **Methemoglobinemia**: inhaled NO and nitrates can oxidize hemoglobin. Methylene blue is the antidote, except in G6PD deficiency; methylene blue also inhibits MAO-A (serotonin syndrome risk with serotonergic drugs).
- **Pulmonary arterial hypertension**: PDE5 inhibitors and riociguat target this pathway, alongside endothelin antagonists and prostacyclin analogs. Riociguat and PDE5 inhibitors are not combined (hypotension).
- **Heart failure**: sacubitril–valsartan increases natriuretic peptide cGMP signaling and reduced mortality versus enalapril (PARADIGM-HF). Because neprilysin also degrades bradykinin, a washout from ACE inhibitors is required to avoid angioedema. BNP rises with neprilysin inhibition, so NT-proBNP is the better monitoring marker.
- **Neurocritical care**: nitroglycerin and nitroprusside increase cerebral blood volume and can raise intracranial pressure, so other agents (nicardipine, clevidipine, labetalol) are often preferred for blood pressure control in intracranial hemorrhage or raised ICP.

keyPoints: Endothelial eNOS makes NO from L-arginine; NO activates soluble guanylyl cyclase → cGMP → PKG → relaxation
Isoforms: nNOS (neurons), iNOS (inflammation, sepsis), eNOS (endothelium)
Nitrates (ALDH2 bioactivation; tolerance), nitroprusside (cyanide), PDE5 inhibitors; never combine nitrates with PDE5 inhibitors
Particulate GCs: NPR-A (ANP/BNP; sacubitril blocks neprilysin), GC-C (linaclotide)
sGC stimulators (riociguat, vericiguat) vs activators (cinaciguat) for NO-insensitive sGC

lessons.title: Kinase Cascades: MAPK, PI3K–Akt and JAK–STAT

levels.kid:
Some signals tell a cell to **grow** or **divide**. These signals pass along a chain of helpers called **kinases**, like a line of dominoes.

The first domino gets pushed, it knocks the next one, and that one knocks the next, all the way to the cell's control center. Then the cell knows: time to grow!

Normally the dominoes only fall when they should. But in some cancers, one domino is broken and keeps falling over and over, so the cell keeps growing when it shouldn't.

Scientists make special medicines that **block just the broken domino**. That can stop the cancer cells from growing.
levels.hs:
Many important signals, such as growth factors, insulin and immune messengers called cytokines, work through **kinase cascades**. A kinase is an enzyme that adds a phosphate group to another protein, turning it on or off. In a cascade, one kinase activates the next, which activates the next, amplifying the signal on its way to the nucleus.

Three major pathways:
- **MAPK pathway** (Ras → Raf → MEK → ERK): tells cells to grow and divide. Mutations in **RAS** or **BRAF** keep it stuck on in many cancers, such as melanoma and colon, lung and pancreatic cancers.
- **PI3K–Akt–mTOR pathway**: controls cell survival, growth and metabolism. Insulin uses it to move glucose transporters into muscle and fat cells. The tumor suppressor **PTEN** normally turns this pathway down.
- **JAK–STAT pathway**: used by cytokines (immune signals). The receptor activates JAK kinases, which activate STAT proteins that travel to the nucleus and turn on genes for inflammation and blood cell production.

Drugs called **kinase inhibitors** (names often end in **-tinib**) block specific kinases. Imatinib blocks the BCR-ABL kinase in chronic myeloid leukemia and transformed that disease into a manageable condition. Vemurafenib blocks mutant BRAF in melanoma. **JAK inhibitors** (names ending in -citinib) such as tofacitinib treat rheumatoid arthritis.

These "targeted therapies" work best when a cancer depends on one broken signal.
levels.college:
**Receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs)** (EGFR, HER2, VEGFR, PDGFR, insulin receptor) dimerize on ligand binding, trans-autophosphorylate tyrosines, and recruit SH2- and PTB-domain proteins.

**MAPK/ERK:** phosphotyrosine recruits Grb2–SOS; SOS (a GEF) loads Ras with GTP. Ras-GTP recruits and activates **Raf** (A-, B-, C-Raf), which phosphorylates **MEK1/2**, which phosphorylates **ERK1/2**. ERK enters the nucleus to activate transcription factors (Elk-1, c-Fos, c-Myc) driving proliferation. NF1 (a Ras GAP) is a tumor suppressor.

**PI3K–Akt–mTOR:** class I PI3K converts PIP2 to **PIP3**, recruiting **Akt** and PDK1. PDK1 phosphorylates Akt at Thr308, and mTORC2 phosphorylates it at Ser473. Akt inhibits GSK-3, FOXO and TSC2; TSC2 inhibition activates Rheb and **mTORC1**, which drives protein synthesis via S6K and 4E-BP1. **PTEN** dephosphorylates PIP3. In insulin signaling, IRS proteins link the insulin receptor to PI3K, and Akt promotes GLUT4 translocation (via AS160).

**JAK–STAT:** cytokine receptors lack intrinsic kinase activity; associated **JAKs** (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, TYK2) trans-phosphorylate on ligand binding, phosphorylate receptor tyrosines, and recruit **STATs**, which are phosphorylated, dimerize and enter the nucleus. **SOCS** proteins provide negative feedback. JAK3 pairs with the common γ chain (IL-2, -4, -7, -9, -15, -21 receptors), so its loss causes SCID; JAK2 serves EPO, TPO and GM-CSF receptors.

**Drugs:**
- EGFR: erlotinib, gefitinib, osimertinib (covers T790M); cetuximab (antibody)
- HER2: trastuzumab, lapatinib
- BCR-ABL: imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib, ponatinib (T315I)
- BRAF V600E: vemurafenib, dabrafenib, encorafenib, combined with MEK inhibitors (trametinib, cobimetinib, binimetinib)
- KRAS G12C: sotorasib, adagrasib (covalent)
- PI3Kα: alpelisib; Akt: capivasertib; mTORC1: sirolimus, everolimus
- JAK: ruxolitinib (JAK1/2), tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib; TYK2: deucravacitinib
levels.phd:
Kinase pathways are wired with **negative feedback**, which shapes both drug response and resistance. ERK phosphorylates SOS, Raf and upstream RTKs, and induces DUSPs and Sprouty proteins. Inhibiting MEK or BRAF relieves these brakes, reactivating RTK and Ras signaling, an adaptive resistance mechanism. In BRAF V600E colorectal cancer, BRAF inhibition relieves feedback on EGFR, so monotherapy fails, while BRAF plus EGFR antibody combinations succeed (BEACON CRC). Similarly, mTORC1 inhibition with rapalogs relieves S6K-mediated inhibitory phosphorylation of IRS-1, activating PI3K and Akt and blunting antitumor effects.

**Paradoxical activation** is another wiring consequence. ATP-competitive BRAF inhibitors bound to one protomer of a Raf dimer allosterically transactivate the other protomer in BRAF-wild-type cells with active Ras. This drives MAPK signaling in keratinocytes, explaining cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas and keratoacanthomas with vemurafenib, which MEK co-inhibition reduces. "Paradox breaker" BRAF inhibitors that disrupt dimerization are in development.

Inhibitor pharmacology has diversified. **Type I** inhibitors bind the active (DFG-in) conformation; **type II** (imatinib) bind the inactive DFG-out state, conferring selectivity; **type III/IV** allosteric inhibitors (trametinib in MEK's allosteric pocket; asciminib in ABL's myristoyl pocket) avoid the conserved ATP site; **covalent** inhibitors target non-conserved cysteines (osimertinib at EGFR C797, sotorasib at KRAS G12C in the switch-II pocket of GDP-bound KRAS). Resistance mutations mirror these binding modes: gatekeeper mutations (T315I in ABL, T790M in EGFR), C797S abolishing covalent binding, and alternative bypass pathways (MET amplification).

**JAK2 V617F** lies in the JH2 pseudokinase domain, which normally autoinhibits JH1; the mutation relieves autoinhibition, causing cytokine-independent signaling in polycythemia vera and other myeloproliferative neoplasms. Deucravacitinib exploits the pseudokinase domain of TYK2 for allosteric, highly selective inhibition.
levels.expert:
Targeted kinase therapy is now routine, and its practical skills are matching the drug to the molecular driver and managing on-target toxicities.

- **Test before treating.** Non-small cell lung cancer is profiled for EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, KRAS G12C, MET, RET, NTRK and HER2 alterations; melanoma for BRAF V600; CML for BCR-ABL with molecular monitoring of response. In neuro-oncology, BRAF V600E–mutant gliomas (including some pediatric low-grade gliomas and gangliogliomas) respond to dabrafenib plus trametinib, and IDH-mutant gliomas to the IDH inhibitor vorasidenib, which is changing postoperative management for neurosurgical patients.
- **On-target toxicities**: EGFR inhibitors cause acneiform rash and diarrhea; VEGFR inhibitors cause hypertension, proteinuria and impaired wound healing (relevant to surgical timing); alpelisib causes hyperglycemia because PI3Kα mediates insulin action; mTOR inhibitors cause stomatitis, hyperlipidemia, impaired wound healing and pneumonitis; MEK inhibitors cause retinopathy, rash and cardiomyopathy.
- **Interactions**: most oral kinase inhibitors are CYP3A4 substrates, and many need acid for absorption, so PPIs reduce exposure of some (dasatinib, erlotinib). QT prolongation occurs with several (nilotinib, vandetanib).
- **JAK inhibitors**: effective in rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ulcerative colitis, atopic dermatitis, alopecia areata and myelofibrosis. The ORAL Surveillance trial (tofacitinib vs TNF inhibitors in older RA patients with cardiovascular risk) found more major cardiovascular events, malignancy, thrombosis and death, leading to boxed warnings and use after TNF inhibitors in many indications. Screen for tuberculosis and hepatitis B, and consider zoster vaccination, because herpes zoster reactivation is a class effect.
- **mTOR in neurology**: everolimus shrinks subependymal giant cell astrocytomas and reduces seizures in tuberous sclerosis complex, a direct application of TSC–mTORC1 biology that can avoid or delay surgery.

Resistance is expected. Repeat biopsy or liquid biopsy at progression guides the next agent.

keyPoints: RTKs dimerize and autophosphorylate; SH2 proteins (Grb2–SOS) activate Ras → Raf → MEK → ERK
PI3K makes PIP3 → Akt (PDK1 Thr308, mTORC2 Ser473) → mTORC1; PTEN opposes; insulin uses this for GLUT4
Cytokines use JAK–STAT; SOCS gives feedback; JAK3/γc loss causes SCID; JAK2 V617F drives polycythemia vera
Targeted drugs: imatinib (BCR-ABL), osimertinib (EGFR), BRAF + MEK inhibitors, sotorasib (KRAS G12C), rapalogs, JAK inhibitors
Feedback relief and paradoxical activation explain resistance and toxicities; JAK inhibitors carry boxed warnings

test.q: Everolimus and sirolimus inhibit the kinase complex ___.
test.explain: With FKBP12, rapalogs allosterically inhibit mTORC1.

test.q: Suppressor of cytokine signaling proteins, abbreviated ___, provide negative feedback on JAK–STAT signaling.
test.explain: STATs induce SOCS, which inhibit JAKs and target receptors for degradation.

kidTest.q: In the story, kinases are like:
kidTest.explain: Each kinase knocks over (activates) the next one.

kidTest.q: What happens in some cancers?
choices: One domino is broken and keeps falling
kidTest.explain: A stuck-on kinase keeps telling the cell to grow.

kidTest.q: What do special cancer medicines do?
kidTest.explain: Targeted medicines block the overactive kinase.

kidTest.q: When the domino message reaches the control center, the cell knows to:
kidTest.explain: The signal tells the cell to grow or divide.

kidTest.q: Enzymes that pass the signal along like dominoes are called ___.
kidTest.explain: Kinases add phosphate groups to switch the next protein on.

advancedTest.q: BRAF inhibitor monotherapy works in BRAF V600E melanoma but poorly in BRAF V600E colorectal cancer, mainly because in colorectal cancer:
choices: BRAF isn't expressed in colon cells, so the drug has no target there
The drug isn't absorbed well by patients with colorectal tumors
MEK is absent in colon cancer cells, so BRAF signals another way
BRAF inhibition relieves feedback and reactivates EGFR signaling
advancedTest.explain: Feedback-driven EGFR reactivation explains why BRAF plus EGFR antibody combinations are used in colorectal cancer.

advancedTest.q: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas during vemurafenib therapy result from:
choices: Loss of PTEN in keratinocytes, which activates PI3K–Akt signaling in the skin
Paradoxical MAPK activation via Raf dimer transactivation in BRAF-wild-type cells
Direct DNA damage by the drug, which absorbs UV light and forms thymine dimers
JAK inhibition in skin immune cells, which removes tumor immune surveillance
advancedTest.explain: Inhibitor binding to one Raf protomer transactivates the other in cells with active Ras; MEK co-inhibition reduces this.

advancedTest.q: Osimertinib resistance via EGFR C797S works by:
choices: Removing the cysteine osimertinib bonds to covalently
Mutating the gatekeeper threonine to methionine
advancedTest.explain: Osimertinib forms a covalent bond with C797; C797S prevents this. T790M is the gatekeeper mutation it was designed to overcome.

advancedTest.q: Rapalog (mTORC1 inhibitor) monotherapy can paradoxically increase Akt activity because:
choices: It inhibits PTEN, so PIP3 builds up and directly activates Akt in the cell
It blocks mTORC2 strongly, which removes Akt's main inhibitory kinase
It relieves S6K-mediated negative feedback on IRS-1, enhancing PI3K signaling
It directly binds and activates Akt in addition to inhibiting mTORC1 itself
advancedTest.explain: Loss of S6K feedback onto IRS-1 increases upstream PI3K–Akt signaling.
